source.title: LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately
source.authors: Jia-Chen Zhao; Jing Huang; Zheng-Xuan Wu; David Bau; Wei-Yan Shi

record.tranche_reason: The study tests related safety behaviors using prompt-template token removal and adversarial fine-tuning, rather than reproducing the original studies’ methods and measures.
record.gate_note: The study reports refusal rates after removing post-instruction template tokens and states that adversarial fine-tuning causes models to start accepting held-out harmful instructions. It does not report harmful-compliance rates for its jailbreak methods, KL by response position, compliant response prefills, or decoding changes. Its latent belief and guard-classification results do not measure the behaviors named by the listed versions; the relevant fine-tuning belief result is recorded under fits_no_version. Steering and reply-inversion outcomes are induced by design and are not evidence of uninduced behavior.
record.test_reason: The study uses a harmful fine-tuning attack (50–400 steered acceptance examples) as a tool to check whether its Latent Guard survives fine-tuning. It reports only its own detector's internal belief score (Figure 7, Appendix H.2). Its only behavioural statement is that the model 'starts to accept held-out harmful instructions', with no compliance rate, no baseline and no named model. That is not enough for a V1 verdict. Other results concern latent harmfulness/refusal representations, steering induced by design, and template-token removal. None of these measures a listed version (no per-token KL, no prefilling, no suffix or decoding attack success rates).
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that harmfulness (encoded at tinst) and refusal (encoded at tpost-inst) are represented separately, and that some jailbreaks suppress refusal without reversing the harmfulness belief. They also conclude that adversarial fine-tuning leaves the harmfulness belief almost unchanged, so Latent Guard is robust to the tested attack. They suggest fine-tuning may mainly affect surface-level response styles, and link this to shallow safety alignment as an open question.
record.recipe_differences: The fine-tuning uses adversarial acceptance examples generated by reverse-refusal steering and response-only loss; the paper does not reproduce the original harmful or benign fine-tuning recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Refusal rates after template-token removal differ across the three models. The adversarial fine-tuning experiment varies the number of examples from 50 to 400.

fits_no_version.finding: After adversarial fine-tuning, the model accepts held-out harmful instructions, yet the tinst harmfulness belief is almost unchanged (Fig. 7). The refusal direction computed after fine-tuning still elicits refusal, slightly weakened with more examples (Fig. 18).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmful fine-tuning changes refusal/acceptance behaviour while leaving internal harmfulness representations largely intact (fine-tuning acts on surface-level refusal).

fits_no_version.finding: Removing post-instruction template tokens lowers harmful-prompt refusal: Llama2 100→85.3%, Llama3 96→58.9%, Qwen2 98→81.3%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal is anchored in post-instruction template tokens (template-anchored safety).

record.problems: The fine-tuning section does not identify the model in the reported text or give numerical held-out compliance rates. Figure 7 provides no numeric values in the text. The main template-token comparison reports refusal rates but no uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No otherwise eligible results left out. The study's jailbreak analysis reports internal harmfulness/refusal beliefs rather than harmful-compliance rates; its induced steering and reply-inversion results are not uninduced behavior.

untested.parts: No harmful-compliance rate, baseline or model identity after harmful fine-tuning; no dose-response in behaviour across 50–400 examples.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
GCG suffixes and jailbreak templates are used, but no refusal or compliance rates are reported; no prefilling or decoding attacks.
Directions in activation space are studied, but no small set of weights or ranks is identified.

missing.what: Appendix H.2 / Figure 18: the refusal direction computed after adversarial fine-tuning still elicits refusal on harmless prompts, with its effect slightly reduced as fine-tuning examples increase.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V1 limits_scope label is unsupported: no number shows any qualification, and the study uses the fine-tuning attack only as a tool. I reclassified the study as T4. The fine-tuning recipe (acceptance responses generated by steering along the reverse refusal direction, response-only loss) differs from the originals. The model fine-tuned is not named in the text.

versions.untested_parts: No numerical harmful-compliance or refusal rates are given after fine-tuning, and the fine-tuned model identity is not stated.
No per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models is measured.

The study does not test compliant response prefills or measure refusal/compliance rates for adversarial suffixes or decoding changes. Removing post-instruction template tokens is a different manipulation.
No small set of weights or ranks is identified as carrying safety behavior.
The study does not test whether data or a training objective causes safety to concentrate in the first response tokens.
No training method designed to deepen safety across response tokens is evaluated.

rows.subject: L LAMA 2-C HAT-7B
rows.operation_detail: Removed post-instruction special tokens from the prompting template.
rows.note: Refusal decreased but remained common. This tests omission of template tokens, not a compliant response opening.
rows.check: Removing post-instruction template tokens is not a compliant prefill, suffix or decoding change, so the row does not bear on V4. The state is relative to the with-tokens baseline only.

rows.operation_detail: Removed post-instruction special tokens from the prompting template.
rows.note: Refusal decreased substantially but remained above half.
rows.check: Same as r1: a template-token manipulation, not a listed V4 intervention.

rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on harmful-instruction/acceptance-response pairs; only response loss was used.

conditions.value: adversarial examples generated by steering harmful instructions along the reverse refusal direction

rows.value: The text states that the model starts to accept held-out harmful instructions after fine-tuning.
rows.note: The reported behavioral change is qualitative; no compliance rate or model identity is supplied.
rows.check: Qualitative only: the text says the fine-tuned model starts accepting held-out harmful instructions, but gives no rate, no pre-fine-tuning baseline and no model identity. The study uses the attack as a robustness test for Latent Guard, not as a test of V1. The state is observed in the qualitative sense, but it is too thin to support a verdict.

rows.subject: LLMs (fine-tuned model identity not stated)
rows.operation_detail: Measured the internal harmfulness belief after adversarial fine-tuning.
rows.value: The text describes the belief as almost unchanged despite the increase in adversarial training examples.
rows.note: The result is stated in the text, but the figure gives no numeric values or model identity.
rows.check: This measures the study's own latent harmfulness belief score, not harmful compliance. Figure 7 gives no readable numeric values or model identity. It belongs under fits_no_version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
